## Findings by module

### cinematography-1

- **confirmed** (ch-007.txt): Where to Go from Here (Film Art): no researcher into perception now accepts persistence of vision; filmic motion happens in the brain through short-range apparent motion, not on the retina; Anderson and Anderson cited. Confirms the refined wording added to module 1.
- **refined** (ch-007.txt): Film Art gives the better account of why moving images look continuous: persistence of vision is a weak explanation; two processes are involved, critical flicker fusion (a light flashed faster than about 50 times a second looks steady) and apparent motion. At 24 fps each frame is projected twice, so the screen flashes 48 times a second; early silents at 16 or 20 fps flickered with one flash per frame, hence 'flickers'. Agrees with the Handbook (48-72 flashes a second) and sharpens its beta-movement wording.
- **refined** (ch-013 speed of motion): Film Art: silent films shot at 16 to 20 fps look jerky at 24 fps; 24 fps standard set with synchronised sound; 35mm cameras offer 8 to 64 fps; ramping, time-lapse and high-speed (hundreds of fps) defined; Ballhaus 24 to 8 fps shutter control in Dracula

### cinematography-4

- **confirmed** (ch-009.txt): Motivation: Film Art defines motivation as the justification a viewer finds for any element, with a candle-lit flicker as the example (production lights stand off screen but the candle purports to be the source); a character crossing the room can motivate a camera move. Supports the course's motivated-light lesson.
- **extended** (ch-012.txt): Four features of lighting: quality (hard or soft), direction (frontal, side or cross, back or rim, under, top), source (motivated by visible lamps and windows) and colour (filters on lights, such as orange for candlelight, or unmotivated colour as Eisenstein's blue). Shadows are attached (shading from the object's own shape, such as the nose on a cheek) or cast (on another surface); highlights show texture. Frontal light removes shadows and flattens; side light sculpts; backlight alone gives silhouette and with front light gives an edge or rim; underlighting distorts (horror, or a flashlight or fire as a real source); top light shapes cheekbones.
- **extended** (ch-012.txt): High-key against low-key: high-key uses fill and backlight for low contrast and soft shadows with detail in the dark areas, and suits comedy, adventure and most drama (even night scenes, as in Back to the Future); low-key uses hard sidelight with little or no fill for chiaroscuro, common in horror and film noir. Three-point lighting is rearranged for each camera position; overlapping several key lights keeps constant lighting on a moving actor (Nights of Cabiria), while moving through dappled light does the opposite (Rashomon). Cinematographers' comments: backlight overused is like too much chili powder.
- **extended** (ch-021 Breathless): Film Art: Breathless shot on location with available light only and hand-held / wheelchair camera (Coutard); jump cuts and mismatched screen direction used deliberately; sound ambient noise left in. Useful as a counterexample to studio three-point lighting
- **extended** (ch-023 lighting history): Film Art: studios moved from glass-roofed daylight to artificial light 1914-17; De Mille The Cheat used one or two hard sources with no fill, sold as Rembrandt lighting; became part of the classical lighting repertoire. Also: Muybridge 1878 glass plate horse series, Marey 1882/1888 film strip cameras, Maltese cross intermittent, celluloid 1889
- **extended** (ch-023 sound-era technology): Film Art: early sound forced cameras into soundproof booths, then blimps allowed dollies; 1930s Technicolor three-strip needed lots of light, which with faster stock and smaller apertures encouraged deep focus (late 1930s trend, Kane 1941); 1940s deep focus gave hard-edged look; neorealism used location and non-three-point lighting, post-synced dialogue
- **note** (ch-007.txt): Case study of Collateral (2004): digital high-definition cameras let the filmmakers shoot Los Angeles at night with little added light; custom electroluminescent panels (ELD) lit the faces in the cab with a very dim diffuse glow; multi-camera shooting of the cab crash gave flexible matching in editing. Useful example that artistic aims can drive new equipment.
- **note** (ch-018 genres): Film Art: genre conventions include characteristic technique (horror and thriller use somber lighting, musicals bright light so choreography reads, action uses rapid cutting); Val Lewton horror by shadow, offscreen sound and reaction. Used only as a lighting pointer for module 4

### cinematography-6

- **confirmed** (ch-007.txt): Film Art states that in most theatres the projector carries film at 90 feet a minute, and that a two-hour feature is about two miles of film. This supports the course's 90 ft/min (from 16 frames to the foot) over the Handbook's 96; trust Film Art and the arithmetic.
- **confirmed** (ch-007.txt): Film Art again uses 90 feet per minute: a 100-minute feature is about 9,000 feet of 35mm, carved from as much as 500,000 feet shot (a ratio of about 55:1 by our arithmetic). It also describes dailies, digital intermediate, interpositive, internegative, answer print and release print routes, confirming the Handbook's hybrid-finish description.
- **extended** (ch-007.txt): Gauges and image quality: picture quality generally rises with film width (35mm better than 16mm, 70mm better than both); Imax prints on 70mm run horizontally with images ten times larger than 35mm and three times larger than 70mm; optical sound tracks (variable-area) sit right in 16mm and left in 35mm; magnetic tracks nearly obsolete; digital tracks encoded as dots near perforations. Shutter admits light only while the frame is still.
- **extended** (ch-013 tonalities): Film Art: contrast depends on stock, light and development; tinting (dye bath, lights coloured) versus toning (darks coloured); hand colouring; day for night with filters; colour timer chooses key tone; overexposure used expressively
- **extended** (ch-013 formats): Film Art: Super 35 expands image area for 2.40 anamorphic or 1.85 matted release; Super 16 gives about 40 percent more image area for 35mm blow-up at 1.85; Edison-Lumiere 1.33 not standardised until 1911

### cinematography-5

- **confirmed** (ch-010.txt): Hitchcock's bomb-under-the-table account (from the Truffaut interviews) appears here too: showing the audience the bomb and the clock turns a trivial conversation into fifteen minutes of suspense against fifteen seconds of surprise. Film Art ties it to range of knowledge: narration that gives the viewer more than the characters know builds suspense (Psycho's Lila in the Bates house), while restricted narration (The Big Sleep) builds curiosity and surprise. Agrees with the Handbook.
- **confirmed** (ch-014 180 degree system): Film Art: axis of action keeps camera on one side; preserves relative positions, eyelines and screen direction; crossing it flips positions and direction and disorients; new axis established when characters re-arrange (Maltese Falcon shot 6)
- **refined** (ch-007.txt): Scheduling: Film Art says many producers try to schedule the most difficult scenes early, before cast and crew tire (Raging Bull's fights were filmed first), and shoot by location for economy; the Handbook advises easier scenes first and no key scene on day one. The two views disagree. The course already shows both; Film Art gives industry examples for hardest-first.
- **extended** (ch-007.txt): Production roles and procedure: director's crew (script supervisor, 1st-3rd AD), photography unit (DP, operator, key grip, gaffer), sound unit (recordist, boom operator, room tone), slate and clapboard, master shot then coverage, A camera and B camera, many cameras for one-off action (Gladiator 7, XXX 13), storyboards and previsualisation (Hitchcock's The Birds storyboard; Revenge of the Sith 6,500 previz shots), rough cut then fine cut (Apocalypse Now rough cut 7.5 hours), half or more dialogue often rerecorded in ADR.
- **extended** (ch-009.txt): Camera height as progression: Lumet shot the first third of Twelve Angry Men above eye level, the second at eye level and the last below it, so the ceiling appeared and the room seemed to shrink (from Making Movies, quoted by Film Art). Also Hitchcock's Rope uses 11 shots and Rear Window limits the action to what the hero can see, as self-imposed formal challenges. Segmentation (outlining a film into numbered parts) is a useful analysis habit for the capstone shot list.
- **extended** (ch-010.txt): Narration terms: story (all events, shown or inferred) against plot (what is on screen) and diegetic against nondiegetic material; range of knowledge (restricted to omniscient) and depth (objective, perceptual subjectivity such as POV shots and sound perspective, mental subjectivity such as memories and fantasies) are independent; POV shots are usually bracketed by objective shots; flashbacks, flash-forwards and screen duration that expands or compresses story time (the bridges in October).
- **extended** (ch-013 framing): Film Art: six zones of offscreen space (Burch); angle, level (canted), height and distance; shot sizes ECU to XLS measured against the body; framing has no fixed meaning, function depends on the film (Kane low angle, North by Northwest high angle); POV shots; framing as motif or rarity; pan and tilt defined
- **extended** (ch-013 mobile frame): Film Art: pan, tilt, track/dolly, crane, Steadicam (Bound for Glory, Rocky, Shining), handheld from cinema verite; zoom changes magnification only while real movement changes relative positions and shows sides of objects (tracking vs zoom test); reframing is unnoticed small pan/tilt; following vs independent camera movement; speed of movement shapes rhythm; motifs of movement (Psycho forward)
- **extended** (ch-013 long take): Film Art: long take is not long shot; average shot length about 5s late 1910s-20s and about 10s after sound; plan-sequence; long takes need dense staging in medium/long shots; 35mm reel about 11 minutes limits Rope (11 shots, hides cuts); digital allowed Russian Ark (single ~90 minute Steadicam take); Touch of Evil opening as a shot with its own arc
- **extended** (ch-013 Grand Illusion and Wavelength): Film Art: camera movement independent of figures reveals information (unrestricted narration) and links characters; Wavelength is a 45 minute zoom where style dominates narrative; colour versus black and white conventions are contextual (1930s-40s colour for fantasy)
- **extended** (ch-014 editing dimensions): Film Art: edits join with cut, fade, dissolve, wipe; four relations between shots: graphic, rhythmic, spatial, temporal; graphic match and graphic discontinuity; rhythm via shot length (Birds: 41s, 13s, 2.3s, 1.5s accelerating; shots 30-40 shortening by 2 frames); Kuleshov effect builds a spatial whole from parts; Hollywood film typically 1000-2000 shots
- **extended** (ch-014 continuity tactics): Film Art: establishing/breakdown/reestablishing shot pattern; shot/reverse shot is not literally reversed, usually 3/4 view of opposite end of axis; eyeline match; match on action carries a movement across the cut; continuity rhythm: long shots held longer than mediums than close-ups; ellipsis by dissolve, empty frame or cutaway; overlapping editing expands time; flashback and flash-forward
- **extended** (ch-014 fine points): Film Art: cheat cuts are tolerated when narrative flow dominates (Jezebel, Falcon chair); axis shifts as characters move (Bringing Up Baby); establishing shot can be omitted via eyelines (She's Gotta Have It); legitimate ways across the axis: on-axis head-on/tail-on shot as transition, symmetrical settings; screen-direction break tolerated when action is clear (Stagecoach); POV cutting stays on looker's side of the axis (Rear Window); Prieto: keep the spirit of the light over strict lighting continuity
- **extended** (ch-014 crosscutting and intensified continuity): Film Art: crosscutting (Griffith, M) gives omniscient narration and simultaneity; temporal continuity cued by no gaps, diegetic sound bleeding over cuts, match on action; intensified continuity: 300-500 shots 1930-60 vs 2000-3000+ now, Bourne Ultimatum average about 2s, tighter framings, telephoto, fewer establishing shots, more camera movement
- **extended** (ch-014 ellipsis and alternatives): Film Art: classic rule dissolve = short lapse, fade = long lapse, modern films use plain cuts with changes of light/place/position; montage sequence compresses time; jump cut = two shots of same subject not different enough in distance/angle, avoided by 30 degree rule; nondiegetic insert; Ozu/Tati use 360 degree space and still stay intelligible; Eisenstein discontinuity; intensified continuity linked partly to television
- **extended** (ch-016 style): Film Art: style is the patterned use of techniques; choose a few techniques and stay consistent; match technique shifts to story progression (Dead Man Walking mesh to longer lenses; Silence of the Lambs camera closer and nearer the axis as intimacy grows); imagine alternatives to judge a choice; Citizen Kane deep focus plus long takes keep an objective view and Welles uses depth, sound and staging instead of cutting
- **extended** (ch-019 documentary): Film Art: documentary can stage events for the camera if the claim stays factual (Fires Were Started, Man with a Movie Camera); direct cinema became possible when portable camera and sound arrived; categorical and rhetorical forms; talking-head framing choices (extreme close-up of mouths in Gap-Toothed Women) are style decisions
- **extended** (ch-021 Raging Bull and Man with a Movie Camera): Film Art: Raging Bull fights use Steadicam, backlight from ring spotlights, slow motion POV, track-forward plus zoom-out (Vertigo effect) for subjectivity; Man with a Movie Camera uses double exposure, pixillation, split images. Sample analyses otherwise criticism-focused, no course change
- **extended** (ch-023 movements): Film Art: Impressionists strapped cameras to cars and locomotives, handheld Debrie camera on roller skates (Napoleon), 2-frame and single-frame cutting in La Roue, subjective POV cutting; Expressionism relies on mise-en-scene and chiaroscuro lighting, carried into noir. Historical colour only
- **note** (ch-012.txt): Film Art on acting (typage, individualised against stylised performance, the eyes and hands, camera distance changing how big the acting must be, editing building composite performances) is relevant to the directing course rather than cinematography; no change here. Cukor staged a five-minute Adam's Rib shot with Hepburn's back to camera so attention fell on Holliday.
- **note** (ch-013 real time): Film Art: Bazin's real-time claim is complicated by digital composites (War of the Worlds van shot) and screen time not equalling story time (Notting Hill 100s covers a year); subjective shot history (Lady in the Lake)
- **note** (ch-014 editing end): Film Art: Eisenstein October sequence shows discontinuity editing (false eyeline match, overlapping cut, frequency ambiguity); modern intensified continuity sometimes crosses the axis when staging is static; Murch: choose shot where actor's eyes register; Thom Noble: editors assemble seven best moments from different takes; Moulin Rouge over 4000 shots
- **note** (ch-015 sound end): Film Art: diegetic vs nondiegetic, onscreen/offscreen, sound perspective, sound bridge and dialogue hook; dubbing vs subtitles; none feeds a visual-only cinematography course beyond a short pointer that sound is half the film (Coppola)

### cinematography-2

- **extended** (ch-007.txt): Digital resolution levels (720p, 1080p, 2K, 4K): each step multiplies the information, so 4K carries four times 2K; 1080p the most used in Hollywood; 4K claimed equal to 35mm; beyond about the sixth row of a theatre the 2K-4K difference is hard to see; consumer cameras compared to Super 8, prosumer to 16mm; professional HD uses low compression and 24 fps with sensors near 35mm frame size. Digital cheaper is disputed (Caché shot with six cameras because they broke).
- **note** (ch-015 sound basics): Film Art: sound is a separate track built independently; loudness suggests distance, pitch, timbre; dialogue recorded for clarity, mics are unselective so sound is selected and cleaned; dialogue overlap smooths shot changes; silence is a tool. Outside the course scope beyond camera-side audio, so no lesson planned

### cinematography-3

- **confirmed** (ch-013 aspect ratio): Film Art: aspect ratio 1.33:1 early, Academy 1.37:1 after sound track added, standard until mid-1950s; early sound about 1.17:1
- **refined** (ch-024 glossary lens and ratio): Film Art glossary: normal lens in 35mm is 35 to 50mm; glossary calls Academy ratio 1.85:1 'currently' whereas the chapter text gives Academy 1.37:1 (1.33 before the sound track) and 1.85 as the widescreen standard. Trust the chapter text, treat the glossary line as loose
- **extended** (ch-007.txt): Image size and exposure shape style: 1920s-50s picture palaces had screens about 50 feet wide, supporting staging with several faces in one frame; television's small early screens pushed close-ups, which spread to cinema; widescreen films shot with a TV safe area encouraged singles; letterboxing approximates theatrical proportions; Kubrick preferred full frame video and Godard composes for full frame; 16:9 is a third wider than 4:3 (16/9 divided by 4/3 = 1.33) and a widescreen TV set wrongly stretched squashes people. Agrees with the course's aspect-ratio lesson and with the Handbook's safe-area advice.
- **extended** (ch-012.txt): Composition and depth cues: balance (loose left-right balance, symmetry, unbalance that primes a change such as a doorway in the background), attention goes to contrast (light on dark, warm colours attract while cool recede, a limited palette makes a stray colour pop), movement (the only moving thing wins), and frontality (faces over backs). Monocular depth cues: overlap, size diminution, linear perspective, aerial perspective (haze, soft focus, desaturation in the distance), shading and cast shadows, movement; stereopsis is the binocular cue added by 3D. Deep-space against shallow-space composition; Mackendrick: in depth, preparation for the next event can be seen behind the current one.
- **extended** (ch-013 focal length): Film Art: on 35mm, under 35mm is wide, about 50mm normal, 100mm+ telephoto; wide exaggerates depth and speeds approach, long flattens and slows approach (Tootsie, The Graduate); Kurosawa Red Beard long lens misleads distance; zoom is changing focal length with fixed camera (Conversation)
- **extended** (ch-013 depth of field): Film Art: shorter focal length gives more depth of field; deep space (staging) differs from deep focus (optics); selective focus and rack focus; deep focus came from faster stock, shorter lenses, stronger light (Kane); small digital chips give extreme depth of field
- **extended** (ch-013 aspect ratios): Film Art: 1.85:1 North American, 1.66 and 1.75 European (16x9 approximates 1.75), 2.35 CinemaScope later 2.40 Panavision anamorphic, 2.2 for 70mm; widescreen by hard matte masking or anamorphic squeeze; shooting full frame shows boom mics in unmasked area; widescreen emphasises horizontals, off-centre composition
